content: The data provided appears to be a detailed report on blood donation, screening, and transfusion practices across various countries from 2011 to 2013. 1. Blood donations, including both whole blood and apheresis, were screened for transfusion-transmissible infections (TTIs) such as HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis, Chagas disease, malaria, and HTLV I/II. However, in some cases, data were not reported or unavailable. 2. In France, from 2011 to 2013, 100% of blood donations were screened for all TTIs, including HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, syphilis, and Chagas disease. 3. In Gabon, 100% of blood donations were screened for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis from 2011 to 2013. However, no screening for Chagas disease was reported in 2011 and 2013. 4. In Gambia, only 5% of blood donations were screened for Chagas disease in 2011, with 146,514 out of 945,782 donations tested. 5. In Zambia, 100% of blood donations were screened for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis from 2011 to 2013. 6. In Zimbabwe, 100% of blood donations were screened for HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and syphilis from 2011 to 2013. 7. The proportion of donations testing positive or reactive for TTIs was expressed as the number of positive cases per 100 donations tested. However, some data were not reported or unavailable. 8. Blood samples that tested reactive for HIV in primary screening were sent to national centers for confirmatory testing. Data excluded indeterminate results, which included 473 cases for HIV, 298 for Hepatitis B, 233 for Hepatitis C, and 130 for syphilis. 9. In some cases, positive results included both serological and nucleic acid testing (NAT) positivity. For example, one NAT-positive but anti-HIV-negative case and five NAT-positive but HBsAg-negative cases were reported. 10. Screening for Chagas disease (T. cruzi antibody) was performed selectively, and donors previously tested were not retested. The denominator for Chagas screening was based only on donors screened during the year. 11. Blood component preparation data from 2011 to 2013 were not consistently reported across all countries. In some cases, only partial data were available. 12. A unit of blood component was defined as the preparation from 450 mL of whole blood donations. A unit of apheresis platelets typically contained 200–450 x 10^9 platelets. 13. In Benin, only three centers prepared blood components by centrifugation, while other hospital blood banks used sedimentation methods for red cell and plasma preparation. 14. In Germany, data from 2013 indicated that 70 blood centers prepared blood components, with 100% of whole blood donations separated into components. 15. In Finland, only solvent-detergent-treated fresh frozen plasma (FFP) was used. 16. In Japan, adult-sized blood bags were 400 mL, but 200 mL bags were also used. For apheresis platelets, 200 x 10^9 platelets were counted as one adult unit, while 400 x 10^9 platelets were calculated as two units. 17. In Uganda, data from 2011 to 2013 showed that seven blood centers prepared blood components, with 60% of whole blood donations separated into components in 2013. 18. In the United Kingdom, data were provided by the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service (SNBTS) and the Welsh Blood Service, with a total collection of 271,262 units reported in one year. 19. In Belgium, data from 2011 to 2013 showed that 114 hospitals performed blood transfusions, with units of whole blood, red cells, platelets, and plasma issued or transfused. 20. In Brazil, data from 2011 indicated that 72 blood centers prepared blood components, with a significant number of units of red cells, platelets, and plasma issued for transfusion.
